keyVerseText: And the Israelitish woman's son blasphemed the name of the LORD, and cursed. And they brought him unto Moses: (and his mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan:)
rootMeaning: The root of דִּבְרִי (Dibrîy) stems from דָּבָר (dâbâr), a Hebrew term rich with meanings related to speech, communication, and matters of importance such as commands, decrees, and counsel. The etymology suggests a connection to 'word' or 'speech,' emphasizing the concept of communication or declaration. This root sense adds a layer of personal identity tied to the notion of 'my word,' which goes beyond a simple name to imply a relational or covenantal significance linked to the spoken or revealed word.
usageInScripture: The term דִּבְרִי appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Leviticus 24:11, where it is used as a proper name referring to an individual from the tribe of Dan. The translation 'of Dibri' indicates possession or lineage, identifying Shelomith as the daughter of Dibri. This singular occurrence shows that the word functions primarily as a personal name rather than a common noun, highlighting its role in genealogical and tribal identity within the biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding דִּבְרִי as a name rooted in the concept of 'word' invites reflection on the importance of God's Word in the life of His people. The personal name connects an individual to the powerful idea of divine communication and covenant relationship. This underscores the biblical theme that God's Word is living and active, shaping identity and community. For the Christian faith, it reminds believers that their identity is ultimately found in the Word of God made flesh in Christ, who is the ultimate revelation of God's will and love.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 24:11 recounts an incident involving the son of an Israelitish woman who blasphemed the name of the LORD and was brought before Moses; the verse notes that his mother's name was Shelomith, daughter of Dibri, from the tribe of Dan. The mention of דִּבְרִי here situates the narrative within a specific family and tribal context, emphasizing the personal and communal dimensions of sin and accountability. The name Dibri, meaning 'my word,' subtly reinforces the gravity of blasphemy against God's name, contrasting human speech with the sacredness of divine revelation.
